title: Trentino, and the Alpine clusters
eyebrow: Forty-nine people · not one register record
dek: A cluster of the name in the Valsugana and South Tyrol that this archive can see, has never tested, and has never had a page for.
lead:
This archive holds **forty-nine people of the name in Trentino and South Tyrol**, and has **never opened a register for any of them**. Every one arrived through the family tree. There is no page here that knows Trentino exists — and until now, no page that admitted it.

They are not claimed as relatives. They are **written down because they are there**, and because an archive that only maps the ground it has walked is telling you about its walking, not about the name.

why.heading: Why this is a blind spot and not a branch
why.text:
The pattern this archive keeps meeting is that a **common patronymic is not a family**. *De Franceschi* means «of the Franceschi» and any Italian parish could mint it independently. Trentino sits on the wrong side of the mountains from Istria, in a different diocese and a different state for most of the relevant centuries.

So the expectation here is the same as for Corsica: **a parallel, not a branch.** What makes it worth a page anyway is that it is **the largest body of people of the name this archive holds with no documentary work behind them at all** — and the only honest thing to do with that is say so in public.

places.heading: Where they are
rows: Births 1856–1911, in one unbroken run, and every single one spelt **Defranceschi**. Only three deaths are recorded. Three women married out of the name into **Zanetti**, **Strosio** and **Varesco** — all Trentino surnames, which is at least internally consistent.

The interesting one. An Italian surname in a **German-speaking parish**, and the given names show it happening: *Katharina Johanna de Franceschi* (1823), *Johann Bapt. Franz* (1838), *Andreas Babtist* (1870), *Rosa Theresia Volser* (1886). The same household writing its children's names in two languages across sixty years.
**1734** — with Fiera di Primiero, the earliest the name is recorded anywhere in this region by this archive.
places.close: The shape is worth noticing: **two eighteenth-century outliers** at Strigno and Primiero, a **gap of a century**, then a dense nineteenth-century cluster at Telve and Laives. That is not a family tree. It is **two separate collections of evidence** that happen to share a region, and nobody has tested whether they join.

laives.heading: What the Laives dates say on their own
laives.text:
Eleven people, and the deaths that are recorded are mostly of the young. **Johann Bapt. Franz, 1838–1847** — nine years old. **Maria Karoline, born and dead in 1873.** **Dominico Andres, 1868–1886** — eighteen. **Andreas Babtist, 1870–1893** — twenty-three.

Against that: **Andreas, 1835–1903**, **Carolina Maria, 1840–1921**, **Franz Giovanni Maria, 1876–1939**. Four children of one generation dead before twenty-five, and three of their elders into their sixties, eighties and beyond.

**This is tree data and it may be wrong.** But it is the only place in this archive where a nineteenth-century household's child mortality is visible as a list rather than as a statistic, and it is worth testing against the actual parish books before anybody builds an argument on it.

brazil.heading: The thing this might explain, and the reason not to say so yet
brazil.text:
The **largest concentration of this surname anywhere on earth is in Brazil** — Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, São Paulo — and this archive's own note on it says the in-law names there are **Marcato, Busatto, Poletta, Raminelli, Barbiero, Negri, Catteri, Facco**: *Veneto and Trentino, not Istrian*.

Trentino sent enormous numbers of people to exactly those Brazilian states from the 1870s. So the tempting sentence is that **this cluster is where the Brazilian one came from**.

**That sentence is not written here.** The roster holds **one** person in Brazil — Rodolpho De Franceschi of Porto Alegre — and one person is not a link. The Trentino emigration to Brazil is documented history; **that these particular Defranceschi joined it is a guess**, and this archive has been caught before dressing a guess as a finding.

alps.heading: Two smaller clusters, in the same breath
rows: Four people, and they are plainly one household: **Pietro (1884–1957)** and **Rosa (1885–1956)**, and two children, **Remo (1919–1975)** and **Margherita (1921–1991)**. Italian-speaking Switzerland, over the border from Lombardy. A whole family, fully dated, and not one document read.
**Pierre Defranceschi, 1818–1853.** One man, thirty-five years old, on the French side of the Geneva border. He is the entire French holding of this archive outside Corsica.
alps.close: Neither is joined to anything. Both are recorded so that they are not «discovered» again in a year's time.

next.heading: What would settle it
rows: **Telve parish registers.** Twenty-four people with a ninety-year run of births is either confirmed or destroyed by one book.
**Laives · Leifers.** A bilingual parish register would show whether the name shifts language with the priest or with the household.
**Strigno and Fiera di Primiero, eighteenth century.** The two oldest entries, and the only ones old enough to bear on where the name came from.
**The Brazilian passenger and naturalisation records**, against Trentino origins — the only way the paragraph above becomes a sentence this archive is willing to write.

source: People from the family's MyHeritage tree, counted out of this archive's own roster on 13 September 2026: 49 in Trentino and South Tyrol, 4 at Giubiasco, 1 at Gaillard. **Not one of them is supported by a register record in this archive**, and the page says so rather than implying otherwise. The Brazilian in-law surnames are quoted from this archive's own note on the Brazil cluster.
